idiom_name: test-only struct with impl Trait returning canned values
implementation_notes: The Rust realization is the classic structure written out: the collaborator is a trait (the Rust book's chapter on defining shared behaviour), and the stub is a test-only unit struct whose impl Trait block returns the canned values - no reflection exists, so no framework can conjure the double, and the compiler proves the trait is fully implemented. Feed it to the SUT as &dyn Trait or as a generic parameter; when the code under test is generic the stub costs no dynamic dispatch at all. mockall's #[automock] generates the same struct plus expect_* helpers, which is what to reach for when call counts or argument matchers matter; for a plain canned answer the hand-written struct is less machinery and reads like production code.
pitfalls: A trait with many methods forces the stub to implement all of them; split the trait at the consumer or give the trait default implementations so the stub stays small.
Passing the stub by value moves it into the SUT, so a test that later inspects a counter cannot - pass a reference or put the state behind interior mutability.
A trait object (&dyn Trait) needs the trait to be object-safe; associated functions or generic methods silently rule that out and force a generic parameter instead.

variants.name: mockall #[automock] with expect_*/.return_const
variants.implementation_notes: mockall generates the stub struct from the trait: #[cfg_attr(test, automock)] before the trait, then let w = MockWarehouse::new(); w.expect_has_inventory().return_const(false). The return_const/returning half is the canned answer, while with(...), times(...) and Sequence add the expectation machinery; keep the expectation half unused and the mock is a stub with a generated implementation. Use it when the trait is large (implementing every method by hand is noise), when the trait or struct is external or has several impl blocks (the mock! macro form), or when the test genuinely needs to assert calls as well. It is the library counterpart of the hand-written struct, and the two can coexist: hand-write the small traits, generate the wide ones.
pitfalls: expect_* sets an expectation as well as an answer: without times(0..) or with(any()) an unexpected call panics even though only a canned value was intended.
#[automock] cannot handle traits with trait bounds, types from other crates, or structs with several impl blocks; the mock! macro is the documented fallback.
Expectations live behind a mutable mock, so the double must be declared mut and passed as &mut (or use the expectation-free return_const path on a shared reference where the signature allows).
